title: Choosing the right Cache-Control
summary: You know HTTP requests, responses, and headers. Learn which Cache-Control to send so pages stay fast without going stale.
objective: Pick Cache-Control headers for a site's HTML, versioned assets, and personalized pages, and predict what a cache will do with them.

hook.prompt: A response arrives with `Cache-Control: no-cache`. What does the browser do with it?

options.text: Never stores it
options.feedback: That's what `no-store` does. Despite its name, `no-cache` is about when a stored copy may be reused, not whether it's stored.

options.text: Stores it, but checks with the server before every reuse
Stores it in the browser only, never in a CDN
options.feedback: That's a different directive, `private`. `no-cache` is about when a stored copy may be reused.

options.text: Reuses it for a short default time, then downloads it again
options.feedback: There's no grace period: a `no-cache` copy is never reused without asking the server first.

hook.explanation: The name misleads: `no-cache` stores the response but won't reuse it unchecked. The first concept shows how that check works, and why it's cheap.

bricks.title: Stale isn't gone: revalidation
bricks.body: A stored response is **fresh** while its age is under `max-age`, and the cache reuses it without asking the server. A shared cache reports time already stored in `Age`; what's left is `max-age` minus `Age`. Once **stale**, the copy is kept and revalidated: the cache sends its `ETag` in `If-None-Match`. Unchanged? **304 Not Modified**, no body, and the copy is fresh again. Changed? A normal 200 with the new version. `no-cache` means: store, but revalidate before every reuse.

term.definition: A conditional request that asks the server whether a stale stored response is still current, so it can be reused without downloading it again.

visual.code:
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "33a64df5"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "33a64df5"
Cache-Control: max-age=3600

bricks.prompt: Your browser gets this response from a CDN. How much longer can the browser reuse it without contacting the server?

visual.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Cache-Control: max-age=604800
Age: 86400

options.text: 6 days
7 days
options.feedback: That's the full `max-age`. The CDN already held the response for a day, and `Age` says so.

options.text: 1 day
options.feedback: That's the `Age`: how long it has already been stored, not how long is left.

options.text: None: a response with an `Age` header is already stale
options.feedback: `Age` only reports time already spent in a cache. It's stale only once `Age` reaches `max-age`.

bricks.hint: Convert both numbers to days, then ask what's left.
bricks.explanation:
Freshness left is max-age minus Age.
604,800 s = 7 days; 86,400 s = 1 day
7 days − 1 day = 6 days

bricks.prompt: A stored copy of `/index.html` with `ETag: "33a64df5"` went stale. Meanwhile someone edited the page on the server. The browser revalidates. What comes back?

options.text: 200 OK with the edited page and a new `ETag`
304 Not Modified
options.feedback: A 304 means the `ETag` still matches. The page was edited, so the server's current `ETag` is different.

options.text: 304 Not Modified with the edited page as the body
options.feedback: A 304 never carries a body. When the content changed, the server sends a full response instead.

options.text: Nothing: the browser reuses its copy because it has an `ETag`
options.feedback: An `ETag` doesn't keep a copy fresh. Once stale, it can't be reused until revalidation says it's current.

bricks.explanation: The browser sent If-None-Match: "33a64df5", but the edited page has a different ETag, so the server sends a full 200 with the new version.

bricks.title: no-cache, no-store, private: three jobs
bricks.body: **`private`**: only the user's browser may store it; shared caches like CDNs and proxies must not, so one user's page can't reach another. **`no-cache`**: may be stored anywhere, but is revalidated before each reuse. **`no-store`**: nobody stores it. It doesn't delete copies already stored, and it switches off features like the back/forward cache. For content that must be current and personal, MDN recommends `no-cache, private` over `no-store`.

term.definition: A cache between clients and the server, such as a proxy or CDN, that stores responses and reuses them for many users.

visual.alt: Table of four directives showing whether the browser and CDN may store the response, and whether it's reused without asking the server.
visual.html:

no-cacheYesYesNever

bricks.prompt: Your account dashboard is personalized through a login cookie, sits behind a CDN, and must always show current data. Which header fits best?

options.text: `Cache-Control: no-cache, private`
`Cache-Control: no-cache`
options.feedback: It keeps the page current, but the CDN is still allowed to store one user's dashboard. Personal content needs `private` too.

options.text: `Cache-Control: private`
options.feedback: It keeps the CDN out, but the browser may reuse a fresh stored copy without asking, so the data can be out of date.

options.text: `Cache-Control: no-store`
options.feedback: It works, but you lose 304s and the back/forward cache. `no-cache, private` gets you current and personal without those costs.

bricks.hint: Check two things separately: who may store it, and when it may be reused.
bricks.explanation: private keeps the CDN from storing one user's dashboard; no-cache makes the browser revalidate each time, so the data stays current and unchanged pages cost only a 304.

bricks.prompt: Your homepage was served with `max-age=86400`. To ship an urgent fix, you switch it to `no-store`. A visitor who loaded it an hour ago follows a link back to it. What do they see?

options.text: The old page, from their stored copy
The fixed page, because `no-store` clears stored copies
options.feedback: `no-store` only stops new copies being stored. It doesn't delete the copy this visitor already has.

options.text: The fixed page, after a quick 304
options.feedback: A 304 would confirm the old copy, not deliver a new one. And while the copy is fresh, the browser doesn't ask at all.

options.text: An error, since the stored copy no longer matches the header
options.feedback: The browser can't know the header changed: it never contacts the server while its copy is fresh.

bricks.hint: Does the browser contact the server at all while its copy is fresh?
bricks.explanation: The copy has 23 hours of freshness left, so the browser reuses it without asking. The server never sees the request, so the new header can't reach it.

bricks.title: Two patterns cover most sites
bricks.body: **Versioned files:** put a version or hash in the URL (`bundle.v123.js`) and cache it for a year: `max-age=31536000, immutable`. When the file changes, its URL changes, so an old copy is never reused for the new file. **Fixed URLs** like the HTML page, `favicon.ico`, or an API endpoint can't be renamed, so send `no-cache` with an `ETag`, plus `private` if the response is personalized.

term.definition: Changing a resource's URL whenever its content changes, so the resource can safely be cached for a long time.

visual.alt: Two cards: index.html gets Cache-Control no-cache with an ETag; bundle.v123.js, referenced by that page, gets max-age=31536000, immutable.
visual.html:
/index.html

Fixed URL

Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: "AAPuIbAO"

/bundle.v123.js

Versioned URL, linked from the page

Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable

bricks.prompt: Your HTML is `no-cache`, but `app.js` keeps one URL and is served with `max-age=31536000`. You deploy new HTML and a new `app.js`. What happens for returning visitors?

options.text: They get the new HTML but may keep running the old `app.js`
They get both new files, because the HTML is revalidated
options.feedback: The HTML is revalidated, but it still points to the same `app.js` URL, and that stored copy is fresh for a year.

options.text: They get the new `app.js`, because its `ETag` changed
options.feedback: An `ETag` is only checked during revalidation, and a fresh copy isn't revalidated.

options.text: They keep both old files until they clear their cache
options.feedback: The HTML is `no-cache`, so it's checked on every visit and the new version arrives.

bricks.hint: Which of the two files does the browser actually check with the server?
bricks.explanation: The no-cache HTML updates, but the same app.js URL is still fresh, so the old script runs with new HTML, which can break the page. A versioned URL avoids that.

bricks.prompt: For each resource, which caching pattern fits?

groups.label: Versioned URL, cached for a year

bricks.explanation: Hashed and versioned names get a new URL when they change, so they cache for a year. The page, favicon, and API keep their URLs, so they revalidate.

challenge.situation: Your news site sends every response, including article pages and `/app.js`, with `Cache-Control: max-age=86400`. Editors complain that corrections take up to a day to appear, and the site sometimes breaks right after a deploy.

options.text: Send article HTML as `no-cache` with an `ETag`. Rename the script on each build (`app.3f9a2c.js`) and cache it with `max-age=31536000, immutable`.
options.outcome: Corrections show on the next visit, usually for the price of a 304. Each deploy's HTML points to a new script URL, so old scripts never run with new pages.

options.text: Lower `max-age` to 60 seconds for everything.
options.outcome: Corrections appear within a minute, but HTML and script can still be out of sync for that minute after a deploy, and a rarely changing script is rechecked constantly.

options.text: Send `no-store` on everything.
options.outcome: Copies already stored still last up to a day. After that, every visit downloads everything in full, with no 304s and no back/forward cache.

options.text: Keep `max-age=86400` and also send `no-cache, private`.
options.outcome: Pages and script stay current, but `private` stops the CDN storing anything, so every reader's request reaches your server, and an unchanging script is rechecked on every visit.

challenge.hint: The HTML and the script have different problems: one needs to be current, the other needs a URL that changes.
challenge.explanation: Two fixes for two problems: no-cache keeps fixed-URL HTML current cheaply, and versioned script URLs let you cache code for a year without mismatches.

takeaways: A stale copy isn't thrown away: with an `ETag`, revalidating it costs only a 304 when nothing changed.
Use `no-cache` for content that must be current, add `private` when it's personalized, and save `no-store` for responses that must never be stored.
Put a version or hash in asset URLs and cache them for a year; send HTML and other fixed URLs `no-cache`.
Before raising a `max-age`, remember you can't recall a copy until it expires.
